recipes.title: Coffee- and Spice-Rubbed Lamb with Coffee-Vanilla Sauce

recipes.title: Roast Leg of Veal with Wild Mushroom Sauce and Walnuts

recipes.title: Grilled Pork Tenderloin with Sun-Dried Cherry-Blood Orange Sauce

recipes.title: Coq au Zin

recipes.title: Grilled Lamb with Roasted Garlic–Mint Sauce

recipes.title: Grilled Flank Steak with Roasted Corn–Pancetta Salsa

recipes.title: Grilled Lamb with Olive Sauce

recipes.title: Sautéed Duck Breasts with Smoked Tomato Sauce

principles.rule: Start with the wine's body and mouthfeel, then choose foods whose weight and texture enhance it.
Consider both the grape's fruit character and the flavours oak ageing adds (toast, vanilla, butter, spice) when choosing food.
Match intensity: delicate whites with delicate dishes like sole, robust reds with hearty braises like osso buco.
Keep basic tastes similar: a sauce should never be sweeter than the wine, and wine acid should equal the dish's acid.
A contrast can work too, e.g. a slightly sweet wine offsetting a salty glazed ham.
High-acid wines (Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Sangiovese, Pinot Noir) balance acidic dishes well.
Walnuts and pecans carry their own tannin and soften the apparent tannin of young Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah and Zinfandel.
Salty foods (anchovy, olives, soy, fish sauce) suit light fruity wines but make tannic reds and oaky whites taste harsher.
Pairings can succeed through similarity (herbal dish with herbal wine) or contrast (light fruity rosé refreshing a rich mole).
Asparagus is hard on wine; if needed, choose high-acid Pinot Gris or Sauvignon Blanc.
Artichokes make wine taste oddly sweet and are best avoided with wine.
Hot chiles exaggerate oak, alcohol and tannin; pick fruity whites or soft fruity reds and dry rosé instead.
Egg yolks coat the palate; Champagne, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Gewürztraminer or fruity Chardonnay stand the best chance.
Most vinegars strip a wine's fruit; balsamic used sparingly is the exception. Keep salad dressings at least three parts oil to one vinegar.
White-wine vinegar dressings suit white wines; red-wine or balsamic vinegar suit reds, though balsamic adapts to whites in salads.
Pickled foods clash with wine, except capers used sparingly with Sauvignon Blanc or Pinot Gris.
Bridge ingredients link dish and wine through shared flavour, body, intensity or taste; small tweaks like Dijon in a red sauce help.
Grilled char echoes the toast of oak barrels, so grilled dishes flatter oaked Chardonnay and most barrel-aged reds.
Roasting's juicy interior softens full-bodied wines and its browned crust connects to barrel-aged flavours.
Roasted garlic, nutty and mellow, is a friendly bridge to most red and white wines.
Sautéing adds fat and mouthfeel that suits oily-textured Chardonnay and helps cut tannin in Cabernet and Syrah.
Braising melds flavours and weight; pair with rich whites (Chardonnay, Viognier) or full reds (Zinfandel, Syrah, Cabernet, Merlot).
Spicy, salty, smoked or heavily seasoned dishes want fruity, lower-alcohol wines; avoid oaky and tannic ones.
Rich, fatty foods suit heavier full-bodied wines such as Chardonnay, Cabernet, Merlot, Zinfandel and Syrah.
Keep a dish's sweetness below the wine's; a squeeze of citrus or dash of vinegar can tame a sweet sauce.
High-acid foods (goat cheese, tomato, citrus) need high-acid wines like Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, some Riesling, Zinfandel, Pinot Noir.
Serve lighter before fuller, dry before sweet, and low-alcohol before high-alcohol wines across a meal.
Taste the wine while finishing a sauce; if it seems too tannic, add citrus zest or nuts to the dish.
Cook with decent wine, ideally the same grape you will drink with the dish.
Poached and steamed dishes suit delicate wines (Pinot Gris, some Riesling); smoked foods suit lighter fruity wines.
Neither food nor wine should overpower the other; aim for synergy, and trust your own palate.
Sparkling wine's bubbles and high acid cleanse the palate, making it ideal with smoky, salty, spicy, Asian and Latin food.
Brut and blanc de noirs sparkling wines are the most flexible through a meal; sparkling rosé suits meat and poultry.
Sec sparkling suits lighter desserts; demi-sec and doux sparkling are true dessert wines.
Sparkling wine is a natural brunch wine and handles egg dishes well; serve it well chilled.
Sauvignon Blanc handles spicy, assertive dishes, soups, salads, goat cheese and tomatoes where Chardonnay fails.
Sauvignon Blanc suits aromatic, tangy, spicier foods; fresh herbs in the dish echo its herbal streak.
Sauvignon Blanc is a good opening wine for appetizers and first courses, and the best white for salads, soups and green vegetables.
For delicate seafood with fresh herbs choose unoaked Sauvignon Blanc or crisp Pinot Gris; oaky wines overwhelm.
Soup and wine is tricky because two liquids at different temperatures confuse the palate; complementary flavours rescue it.
Roasting vegetables brings out sweetness that suits Sauvignon Blanc.
With an oaky Chardonnay, cut the chile in a dish, because heat clashes with oak.
If serving a dish with Pinot Noir instead of a white, cook its sauce with red wine rather than sherry.
Pinot Gris is like Sauvignon Blanc without the herbal side; its acidity suits seafood needing more acid than most whites offer.
Pinot Gris/Grigio's mineral, brisk acidity counters fattier seafood and acidic foods like tomato, and copes with spicy dishes.
Lean Italian Pinot Grigio suits light dishes and delicate shellfish; fuller Oregon and Alsace Pinot Gris can handle salmon and sea bass.
Pinot Gris/Grigio is an all-purpose wine for appetizers, lunches and warm weather.
Riesling's forward fruit, crispness and low alcohol make it superb at the table, and good Riesling ages well.
German Riesling: Kabinett for appetizers including spicy ones; Spätlese for Asian food and seafood or poultry in cream sauce.
Riesling and Gewürztraminer, fruity and unoaked, are very flexible with spicy Asian and Latin dishes.
Riesling handles smoked and salty foods, flatters fruit salads and dishes with fruit sauces.
Riesling is a good opening wine, and can contrast hearty dishes through lighter weight; ideal for summer outdoors.
Even with a fruit soup, adjust the dish so it is not sweeter than the wine.
Gewürztraminer and Riesling succeed with smoked, spicy, salty and slightly sweet dishes where other wines fall flat.
Gewürztraminer is low in acid; avoid very acidic dishes, which make it taste lifeless.
Gewürztraminer overwhelms delicately flavoured seafood or poultry; serve it well chilled.
Viognier is full, high-alcohol and low-acid; pair with aromatic, full-flavoured, somewhat rich foods.
Smoky dishes and dishes featuring peach or apricot support Viognier beautifully.
Chardonnay is perhaps the hardest wine to pair: high alcohol and heavy oak; unoaked or lightly oaked versions are far easier.
Heavily oaked, buttery Chardonnay works best as an aperitif or with simply prepared seafood and lighter meats.
Match Chardonnay mainly on texture: dishes of similar weight and creaminess succeed more reliably than flavour matches.
Avoid chile-spicy dishes with Chardonnay; heat accentuates its alcohol and oak.
Toasted nuts sprinkled on a dish draw it toward an oaky Chardonnay; butter and cream also love it.
Corn and tarragon are secret-weapon ingredients for Chardonnay.
Crisp, higher-acid Chardonnay such as Chablis suits silky oysters, especially with a little cream.
Side ingredients can redirect a pairing: creamy beans and smoky pancetta steer tuna from Pinot Noir to oaked Chardonnay.
White wine can match meat: braised pork with apples and cream suits round, barrel-aged Chardonnay.
Dijon mustard used sparingly is a versatile bridge to many wines, Chardonnay included.
Lighter, fruit-forward Pinot Noir is especially food-friendly; fruity styles even handle seasoned, smoked and mildly spicy dishes.
Pinot Noir is the most flexible red: meat, poultry, vegetarian dishes and some fish such as salmon and ahi.
Lightly aromatic spices harmonise with fruity Pinot Noir; don't overwhelm it with powerful, assertive dishes.
Oily, meaty fish like salmon and tuna have enough fat to coat the tongue and balance a red wine's tannin.
Coffee and vanilla in a sauce heighten almost any red wine, especially ones with some bottle age.
Walnuts soften tannins in young reds and add crunch.
Sangiovese's cherry fruit, acidity and grip suit tomato pastas, grilled meats, sausage, poultry, game and garlicky rustic Italian food.
Sangiovese connects best with simple rustic grilled or roasted dishes; avoid rich intense sauces except with Super Tuscans and Brunello.
Fresh herbs bring out Sangiovese's country character; tomatoes are an excellent bridge.
Sun-dried cherries are a near-universal bridge to reds (Sangiovese, Cabernet, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Merlot), amplifying their cherry fruit.
Zinfandel's berry fruit and lively acidity suit grilled meats and spicier food, especially Latin-style dishes.
Very high-alcohol Zinfandel is less food-friendly; too much chile heat clashes with its alcohol.
Zinfandel handles salty dishes better than most reds because its sweet berry fruit contrasts salt.
Match Zinfandel with weightier braised, grilled or smoked dishes and with berry-based fruit sauces.
Syrah: full, round, low-acid, polished tannins; its smoky, peppery, gamey fruit suits meat, game and hearty fare.
Petite Sirah is a different grape from Syrah but pairs with food much the same way.
Syrah shines with robust braises and all kinds of grilled meats; Rhône blends are softer and handle spicier dishes.
Dry rosé is a chilled warm-weather wine for alfresco meals, cold summer dishes and spicy food.
Syrah is the most peppery red, so it marries peppery, intense sauces especially well.
Merlot is often more food-friendly than Cabernet: smooth, round, bright fruit that fits a wide range of foods.
Heavily oaked, tannic Merlot is harder to pair young; Bordeaux blends follow the food affinities of their main grape.
Merlot suits medium-weight dishes more than very heavy food; cooking with Merlot in sauces helps mirror the wine.
A sprinkle of walnuts or pecans reduces the impression of tannin in tannic Merlot.
Colour can help: a deep red dish creates a subconscious link to a red wine.
Keep a fruit sauce less sweet than the wine or the wine seems dry and lifeless; adjust port and sugar to taste.
Soft, supple Merlot suits braises that combine many complementary flavours.
Young Cabernet's power and tannin are hard on food; age brings elegance and better compatibility.
Cabernet generally does poorly with seafood, spicy food and vinegar, except careful use of balsamic.
Match Cabernet to high-quality meat, game or cheese in dishes with focused flavours so the wine is the star.
Fatty meats coat the palate and shield it from young Cabernet's tannin.
Older, mellower Cabernet suits less intense dishes; heavy reduction sauces suit young Cabernet better.
Dishes with a single clear flavour focus show Cabernet best; walnuts and pecans tame young tannins.
Creamy, rich blue cheese like Gorgonzola helps tame a young, tannic Cabernet.
Slight bitterness, as in eggplant, can offset red wine tannin.
Match intensity: an intense balsamic-mushroom sauce parallels a concentrated Cabernet or Syrah.
Earthy porcini mushrooms mellow Cabernet's tannin; juicy lamb supplies flavour and fat.
Taste the sauce with the wine you'll serve; add a touch of balsamic if the sauce is sweeter than the wine.
Dijon mustard and rosemary are especially flattering to Cabernet.
Dessert wines come from very ripe, often botrytised grapes; a 3-4 ounce pour is plenty, and half bottles suit small groups.
Late-harvest Riesling, low in alcohol, is easier to drink after a meal than port and suits delicate desserts.
Don't make the dessert much sweeter than the wine, or the wine tastes dry.
Build menus on contrast and balance: alternate rich courses with lighter or piquant ones rather than stacking richness.
